name: Areca palm leaf sheath
origin: Dried leaf sheaths shed by areca palms; the sheath is cleaned and formed into rigid items.
characteristics: Moulded sheath products are generally rigid and have natural variation in colour and texture. Actual tolerances depend on source and forming process.
processing: Collection, cleaning, drying, heat-and-pressure forming, trimming and packing are described in Government of India project material. Supplier process and hygiene controls must be confirmed.
applications: Plates, bowls and trays are common product examples.
packaging: Rigid food-service ware; confirm intended food contact, coatings, dimensions and test documents.
durability: Single-use serving products are not comparable with reusable fibre goods. Confirm intended use and load.
water: Liquid tolerance varies by construction and coating; request supplier test evidence.
endoflife: Do not assume compostability in every setting. Verify the complete product and local collection/composting route.
environment: Use of fallen leaf sheath is described in government project material; actual sourcing, transport, processing and end-of-life impacts depend on supplier and market.
limitations: Natural shape/colour variation, moisture exposure, food-contact requirements, coatings, packaging and destination rules need review.
source: KVIC Areca Leaf Plates project profile

name: Sugarcane bagasse
origin: Fibrous residue remaining after sugarcane juice extraction.
characteristics: A variable lignocellulosic residue. Moisture, residual sugars and fibre content vary with mill and processing.
processing: Potential paths include drying, pulping or moulding; industrial process and additives vary. Much bagasse is used as mill fuel, so availability is local and competing uses matter.
applications: Fibre-based packaging and tableware are possible product categories; confirm the supplier process and specification.
packaging: Can be formed into fibre-based packaging; food-contact suitability, barriers and heat performance are product-specific.
durability: Strength and moisture performance depend on density, binder, geometry and finish.
water: No universal water-resistance claim; coatings may change recyclability and end-of-life.
endoflife: Compostability depends on the complete item, certification and local facility acceptance.
environment: Use as a by-product does not alone prove lower life-cycle impact; collection, energy, chemicals, coatings and competing uses matter.
limitations: Seasonal/local supply, moisture, odour, additives, food-contact compliance, performance and local waste routes.
source: FAO: Sugarcane as feed (bagasse description and uses)

name: Green coconut residues
origin: Coconut processing residues can include husk, shell and other fractions; these are distinct feedstocks and should not be treated as one material.
characteristics: Properties depend on the fraction: husk contains coir fibre and pith; shell is a separate hard fraction. Moisture and contamination vary.
processing: Dehusking and separation precede fibre or pith processing. Confirm which fraction, maturity, washing, drying and treatment is supplied.
applications: Potential uses depend on the fraction, such as fibre, pith-based growing media or shell-derived products; no availability claim is made.
packaging: Suitability requires a defined fraction and converted product specification; no generic packaging performance is assumed.
durability: Depends entirely on the derived product and processing.
water: Not rated without a product-level test.
endoflife: End-of-life depends on binders, coatings and product construction; do not infer compostability from plant origin.
environment: Using a residue may compete with existing local uses. Assess sourcing and transport rather than assuming a net benefit.
limitations: Feedstock ambiguity, high moisture, storage, contamination, competing uses and product conversion requirements.
source: Coir Board of India: coconut and coir resources

name: Coconut coir
origin: Fibre extracted from the coconut husk; coir pith is the spongy fraction that binds fibres in the husk.
characteristics: Natural fibre with grades and properties that vary by extraction, cleaning, length and moisture.
processing: Husk separation, retting or mechanical defibering, cleaning, drying, grading and conversion into yarn, mats or other goods.
applications: Rope, yarn, mats, brushes, padding and horticultural products are documented applications.
packaging: May be used as cushioning or sacking in some product formats; confirm exact format and test performance.
durability: Fibre quality and durability depend on grade, treatment and intended exposure.
water: Coir is not waterproof; moisture and mould risk require storage and shipment controls.
endoflife: Natural fibre content alone does not establish compostability of a finished item; coatings, latex binders and disposal matter.
environment: Environmental performance needs product-specific life-cycle evidence.
limitations: Grade variability, dust/pith, moisture, processing, binders and bulky freight volume.
source: Coir Board of India: Fibre and uses

name: Jute
origin: Bast fibre extracted from the stems of Corchorus plants.
characteristics: Coarse natural fibre used as yarn, woven fabric and diversified goods. Strength, colour and moisture behaviour vary by grade and construction.
processing: Stem harvesting, retting, fibre extraction, washing/drying, spinning or weaving, then finishing and product manufacture.
applications: Bags, baskets, textiles, geotextiles and diversified products are documented examples.
packaging: Used in sacks and reusable bags; suitability depends on weave, seams, coating and intended moisture exposure.
durability: Depends on fibre grade, weave, stitching, abrasion and storage conditions.
water: Absorbs moisture; wet strength, mildew and colour-fastness need product-specific checks.
endoflife: No blanket claim for finished products; dyes, laminates, coatings, trims and local waste routes affect disposal.
environment: A plant-derived fibre does not by itself prove environmental superiority; farming, retting water, processing, durability and reuse matter.
limitations: Moisture sensitivity, natural variation, odour, finish consistency and performance of sewn/laminated products.
source: National Jute Board resource: Jute and Jute Geotextiles

name: Leather
origin: Animal hide or skin processed into a durable material; species, source and tanning process vary.
characteristics: A broad material class with substantial variation in thickness, finish, flexibility, grain and performance.
processing: Hide preparation, tanning and finishing; chemical management, water use, traceability and subcontracting are supplier-specific.
applications: Bags, accessories and other goods; confirm product design, finish and test specifications.
packaging: Leather goods may use paper/textile packaging. Leather itself is generally not used as commodity packaging.
durability: Potentially durable in suitable construction and care; test abrasion, colour transfer, flex and hardware at product level.
water: Water resistance depends on tanning and finish; do not infer it from the word leather.
endoflife: Tanning, coatings, adhesives and mixed materials affect recovery and disposal; avoid generic biodegradability claims.
environment: Leather production impacts vary by raw-material sourcing, tannery controls, chemicals, energy and product life. Audits cover specified facility/process scopes, not every product claim.
limitations: Animal-origin disclosure, traceability, restricted substances, tannery documentation, finish variation and care requirements.
source: Leather Working Group: Manufacturer Standard and audit scope
